entries.title: Climate risk reaches households through land, water and roads
entries.text: UNDP identifies glacial-lake outburst floods as risks to homes and livelihoods in northern Pakistan. Damage to irrigation, farms and transport can disrupt income, schooling and access to services. These are plausible pressures on where households live; this source does not quantify the share of GB population change caused by climate change.
entries.evidence_status: Official programme evidence; mechanism, not migration attribution
entries.scope: GB and KP; regional programme totals are not GB-only

entries.title: Displacement requires durable services
entries.text: An EU-supported project specifically addresses displacement-affected communities in Gilgit-Baltistan through preparedness, infrastructure and integrated services. It identifies gaps in durable settlement planning. A project description establishes a documented policy concern, not a measured GB-wide displacement rate.
entries.source_title: European Commission — Strengthening communities facing climate-related displacement
entries.evidence_status: Official project description; no GB-wide population estimate

entries.title: Glacier change varies across the mountains
entries.text: A 2020 scientific review documented balanced or slightly positive glacier mass budgets in parts of the Karakoram during the preceding decades, alongside glacier surges. This historical variation means a single claim that every GB glacier is retreating is too simple. The review does not establish the condition of every glacier in 2025.
entries.source_title: Farinotti et al. (2020) — Manifestations and mechanisms of the Karakoram glacier Anomaly
entries.scope: Karakoram, not all GB glaciers individually

entries.title: Education and work connect mountain households to cities
entries.text: Research on Karakoram livelihoods describes education, professional employment and income earned away from agriculture as parts of households’ strategies. Family members can live in several places and remain economically connected. Moving away therefore does not always mean permanent separation from a home village.
entries.source_title: Benz (2014) — Mobility, multilocality and translocal development
entries.evidence_status: Peer-reviewed local livelihood research; no current regional rate

entries.title: Documented destinations, without invented flows
entries.text: A study based on 2011–2012 fieldwork in Gojal describes educational connections to Karachi, Gilgit, Islamabad/Rawalpindi, Lahore and Peshawar, and some international family-linked moves. These examples document pathways; they are not a current destination ranking or the percentage of GB youth leaving.
entries.evidence_status: Peer-reviewed local fieldwork; historical destination examples
entries.scope: Hussaini and Passu / Gojal; not representative of all GB

entries.title: Who can move matters as much as who wants to
entries.text: Research in Hussaini and Passu shows that kinship support, gender norms and position within a household shape access to education and jobs elsewhere. Mobility can improve opportunities while widening inequalities between people with different resources. A preference to migrate should not be confused with the ability to do so.
entries.source_title: Benz (2018) — Mobility (in)justice, positionality and translocal development in Gojal
entries.evidence_status: Academic book chapter using local fieldwork; interpretive evidence

entries.title: A city comparison needs services and exposure
entries.text: A 2025 study of Gilgit combines land-cover analysis with expert interviews and discusses pressure on resources and hazard exposure as the city expands. A useful comparison of living conditions should examine education, health, housing, water, employment and disaster risk separately; this study does not support a single universal best-place ranking.
entries.source_title: Shah et al. (2025) — Urbanization, climate change and environmental sustainability in Gilgit
entries.evidence_status: Peer-reviewed city case study; mixed-method evidence
entries.scope: Gilgit city, not whole district or GB

entries.title: Built-up growth is not a population counter
entries.text: Research in selected urbanizing sites in Ghizer, Hunza and Nagar documents land-use and land-price changes using 2009, 2014 and 2019 reference years. It supports studying housing and agricultural-land pressure alongside demography. Built-up expansion alone cannot reveal how many residents moved in or why.
entries.source_title: Ali et al. (2021 online / 2022 volume) — Factors shaping economics of land use change
entries.evidence_status: Peer-reviewed mixed-method local study; observational evidence
entries.scope: Selected sites in Ghizer, Hunza and Nagar

key_limitations: No verified GB-wide causal estimate links climate change to total population change.
No verified current percentage of GB youth migrating, destination distribution, or overseas emigration rate was established.
Historical local case studies must not be shown as representative 2025 statistics.
Migration can be temporary, circular, educational, labour-related, family-related or displacement; keep these categories separate.
UNDP regional exposure and beneficiary totals cover both GB and KP and must never be relabeled GB-only.
Literacy comparisons require matching age groups, sex categories, reference years and definitions.
